notes:
Task and constraints: Split a nonnegative array into exactly k nonempty contiguous parts while minimizing the largest part sum; candidate maximum sums lie between max(nums) and sum(nums).
Idea: lo starts at the largest element and hi at the total sum. For each midpoint, a greedy scan starts a new part whenever adding x would exceed mid. If this needs more than k parts, lo increases; otherwise hi decreases.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search works because feasibility is monotonic: if a maximum sum permits at most k parts, any larger bound also permits it.
Invariant: The optimal largest sum remains within [lo,hi], and the scan computes the minimum number of parts needed under the current bound.
Edge cases: A single element returns itself; all zeros converge to zero; a large element sets the lower bound so no part can have a smaller maximum. Nonnegative values are required for greedy feasibility.
Complexity: Each feasibility check is O(n) and binary search takes O(log(sum(nums))) iterations; auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each binary-search iteration scans nums once and updates only bounds, part count, and current sum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Minimize the largest sum when splitting a nonnegative array into k nonempty contiguous subarrays; use long bounds to safely accumulate sums.
Idea: The first loop finds maximum element lo and total hi. Each midpoint is tested by greedily starting a new part when sum+x exceeds mid. More than k parts raises lo; otherwise hi becomes mid, and the converged bound is cast to int.
Technique and why it applies: Monotone feasibility enables binary search because increasing the allowed maximum cannot increase the minimum number of parts required.
Invariant: The answer stays inside [lo,hi], and parts is the number of segments the greedy scan needs to keep every sum at most mid.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns its value; zero-valued arrays converge to zero; a single large element determines the minimum bound. Nonnegative input makes the greedy scan valid, and long avoids intermediate sum overflow under expected constraints.
Complexity: O(n) per check across O(log(sum(nums))) checks, with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The initialization and each feasibility check scan the array, while only a fixed number of long and int variables are maintained.

notes:
Task and constraints: Produce strings for integers 1 through n, replacing multiples of 3 with Fizz, 5 with Buzz, and both with FizzBuzz.
Idea: The loop checks each i in order. It tests divisibility by 15 first, then 3, then 5, otherwise appending str(i) to out.
Technique and why it applies: Direct simulation mirrors the rules; checking 15 first prevents numbers divisible by both 3 and 5 from being labeled only Fizz.
Invariant: After processing i, out contains exactly the required representation for each integer from 1 through i.
Edge cases: n=0 returns an empty list; 3 becomes "Fizz"; 5 becomes "Buzz"; 15 becomes "FizzBuzz" because the combined condition is tested first.
Complexity: The loop does constant work per integer, giving O(n) time; the returned list stores n strings, using O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The loop appends one result for each integer from 1 through n, so both processing and output storage scale linearly.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return representations for 1..n using Fizz for multiples of three, Buzz for multiples of five, and FizzBuzz for multiples of both.
Idea: The loop checks i%15 first, then i%3, then i%5, appending the corresponding string or Integer.toString(i) to out.
Technique and why it applies: Ordered divisibility checks implement the rule directly, with the combined multiple handled before either individual multiple.
Invariant: After iteration i, out has exactly i entries, each correctly representing its corresponding integer from one through i.
Edge cases: n=0 yields an empty list; 3 and 5 use their individual labels; 30 uses FizzBuzz because the first condition matches. The loop starts at one and includes n.
Complexity: Constant work per integer gives O(n) time, and the output list stores O(n) strings.
complexity_reason: The method iterates through n integers and retains one output string per integer.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count contiguous arithmetic slices of length at least three, where each adjacent difference matches; only adjacent values are compared.
Idea: total accumulates all slices and curr counts arithmetic slices ending at the current index. If the latest two differences match, curr increases and is added to total; otherwise curr resets to zero.
Technique and why it applies: Suffix DP counts every arithmetic slice ending at i by extending each valid slice ending at i-1 and adding the new length-three slice.
Invariant: After processing index i, curr is the number of arithmetic slices ending at i, and total is the count across all processed positions.
Edge cases: Fewer than three values returns zero; [1,2,3] adds one slice; [1,2,3,4] adds one at index 2 and two at index 3, totaling three. Differences may be negative as long as they match.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and two counters give O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Each index from 2 onward compares two differences and updates curr and total, using constant state.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count contiguous subarrays of length at least three with equal adjacent differences; the solution stores only a running suffix count and total.
Idea: For each i from 2 onward, matching differences increment curr and add it to total; a mismatch resets curr to zero. The method returns total after the scan.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming counts the arithmetic slices ending at each position by extending the previous valid suffixes.
Invariant: curr counts arithmetic slices ending exactly at the current index, while total sums those counts over all indices visited.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero; three equally spaced values produce one slice; four equally spaced values produce three total slices. Java int subtraction and total rely on the problem's bounds to avoid overflow.
Complexity: Each index is checked once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The loop visits each index from 2 onward and maintains only two int counters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the third distinct maximum, or the maximum if fewer than three distinct values exist; duplicate values must not fill multiple ranks.
Idea: top stores at most three values. Each x already in top is skipped; otherwise x is appended, top is sorted descending and truncated to three. The method returns top[2] if three distinct values were found, else top[0].
Technique and why it applies: Maintaining only the three largest distinct candidates bounds storage while repeated sorting keeps their rank order explicit.
Invariant: After each number, top contains the largest up to three distinct values seen so far, in descending order.
Edge cases: Repeated maxima are ignored; fewer than three distinct values returns the maximum; negative numbers are handled because no numeric sentinel is used. Input is assumed nonempty.
Complexity: The list never exceeds four elements before truncation, so each iteration does constant-size work and total time is O(n); auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The input is scanned once and top is sorted only while holding at most four values, so extra space is constant.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the third distinct maximum, falling back to the maximum if fewer than three distinct values exist; values may include Integer.MIN_VALUE.
Idea: a, b, and c track the three largest distinct values using Long.MIN_VALUE as an absent sentinel. Each x matching a stored value is skipped; otherwise it shifts larger maxima down or replaces c. The result is c unless c remains the sentinel.
Technique and why it applies: Three scalar maxima maintain the needed ranking without storing or sorting the full array; long sentinels distinguish an absent rank from any int value.
Invariant: a>=b>=c among the distinct maxima currently represented, and each is updated only when x is not already one of them.
Edge cases: Duplicate values do not change ranks; fewer than three distinct values returns a; Integer.MIN_VALUE is valid because it differs from Long.MIN_VALUE. Empty input is outside the usual constraints.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and three long variables use O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The method visits each array value once and maintains only three long-valued maxima.

notes:
Task and constraints: Add two nonnegative decimal strings without converting either entire value to an integer; work depends on the longer string length.
Idea: i and j start at the final digit positions. Each loop reads available digits or zero, adds them with carry, appends total%10, sets carry=total//10, and moves both indices left. The reversed output digits are joined at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Grade-school addition processes least significant digits first, so each step needs only two digits and a carry.
Invariant: After each iteration, out contains the computed result digits from least significant upward for the suffixes already consumed, and carry is the value passed to the next column.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths use zero for a missing digit; a final carry creates one more digit; leading zero input is handled by the digit arithmetic but the output is not explicitly normalized. Empty strings are outside the usual constraints.
Complexity: Each input digit is visited once, giving O(max(n,m)) time and output storage of the same order.
complexity_reason: The loop consumes digits from both strings once and stores one output digit per addition step.

notes:
Task and constraints: Add two nonnegative integers encoded as decimal strings without parsing them as whole numeric values; the output length is at most one digit longer than the longer input.
Idea: i and j walk backward through num1 and num2. Missing digits contribute zero; sum combines both digits and carry, appends sum%10 to StringBuilder out, and updates carry=sum/10. Finally out.reverse().toString() returns the result.
Technique and why it applies: Digit-by-digit addition avoids fixed-width integer limits and mirrors manual decimal addition from right to left.
Invariant: out holds the computed low-order digits in reverse order, and carry represents the amount passed into the next more significant column.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths are padded conceptually with zeros; a final carry adds another digit; charAt is guarded by i>=0 or j>=0. The method assumes nonempty valid decimal strings, and StringBuilder avoids repeated immutable concatenation.
Complexity: The loop takes O(max(n,m)) time and StringBuilder uses O(max(n,m)) space.
complexity_reason: Each input digit is read once and each result digit is appended once to StringBuilder out.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether nonnegative numbers can be split into equal-sum subsets; an odd total immediately makes the partition impossible.
Idea: total is summed and target is total//2. dp[0] is true; for each x, sums descend from target to x and dp[s] becomes true if it was already true or dp[s-x] was true.
Technique and why it applies: One-dimensional 0/1 subset-sum DP records reachable totals; descending iteration ensures each input number is used at most once in this iteration.
Invariant: After processing a prefix of nums, dp[s] is true exactly when some subset of that prefix sums to s.
Edge cases: Odd totals return false; an empty array has target zero and returns true; a value larger than target causes no inner-loop iterations. Nonnegative inputs are required for this recurrence.
Complexity: Each of n values updates up to target states, giving O(n·target) time and O(target) space.
complexity_reason: For every number, the code scans reachable-sum states downward; dp has target+1 boolean entries.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether an int array can be partitioned into two equal-sum subsets; if the total is odd, no such split exists.
Idea: The first loop computes total. dp[0] is true, and for each x the inner loop runs downward from target to x, setting dp[s] if s was reachable or s-x was reachable.
Technique and why it applies: Descending 0/1 subset-sum DP ensures a value contributes at most once, since dp[s-x] has not yet been updated for the current value when s decreases.
Invariant: After each processed element, dp[s] records whether some subset of the processed prefix sums to s.
Edge cases: Odd totals return false; an empty array returns true because target zero is reachable; x>target skips the inner loop. Java int total can overflow only outside the usual problem bounds.
Complexity: The nested loops cost O(n·target) time and the boolean array uses O(target) space.
complexity_reason: Each array element scans the target range downward and dp stores one boolean per subtotal.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return matrix cells from which water can flow to both oceans by moving to equal or lower heights; the method reverses the direction of reachability from ocean borders.
Idea: Empty dimensions return []. dfs marks a cell in a seen set and visits neighbors whose height is at least the current height. Calls from Pacific borders populate pac and calls from Atlantic borders populate atl; the final comprehension returns cells in both sets.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse DFS follows nondecreasing heights inward, identifying every cell that can drain outward to each ocean.
Invariant: Each seen set contains exactly cells reachable from its ocean border under reversed flow rules, and a cell is visited only once per ocean.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; a one-cell matrix belongs to both sets; equal-height neighbors are traversed. The code assumes rectangular rows and uses recursion that may become deep on large grids.
Complexity: Each cell is visited at most once for each ocean, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) set/recursion space.
complexity_reason: Two DFS traversals each mark at most mn cells, and the seen sets plus recursive calls use O(mn) space.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find cells that can reach both Pacific and Atlantic edges while water flows only downhill or level; the code performs reverse searches from each ocean.
Idea: Empty dimensions return an empty list. p and a are boolean matrices. dfs starts from each border, marks the cell, and recursively visits in-bounds neighbors at least as high. A final nested loop adds coordinates marked in both matrices.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse reachability turns the original downhill question into uphill-or-level searches from the destination borders.
Invariant: p[r][c] and a[r][c] indicate reachability from the corresponding ocean under reversed flow; each dfs call stops at already-marked cells.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; a single cell is reachable from both oceans; equal heights are allowed. The recursive implementation can reach O(mn) depth on a large monotone grid.
Complexity: Each cell is visited once per ocean, so time is O(mn); two boolean matrices and recursion use O(mn) space.
complexity_reason: Each ocean's DFS marks each cell at most once; the boolean matrices and recursive stack are O(mn).

notes:
Task and constraints: Count straight battleships represented by X cells; ships do not touch, so each ship has a unique top-left segment cell with no X directly above or left.
Idea: Empty boards return zero. The nested loops skip non-X cells and any X with an X above or to its left; remaining cells increment count.
Technique and why it applies: Counting only segment starts avoids flood fill or modifying the board because non-touching straight ships have one top-leftmost cell.
Invariant: count equals the number of ship starts encountered in the scanned prefix; every ship contributes exactly once at its first row/column cell.
Edge cases: An empty board returns zero; a single X counts as one; horizontal or vertical runs count only at the first cell. The method assumes ships are straight and do not touch as specified.
Complexity: Every cell is checked once for O(mn) time and only a counter is added, giving O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops inspect each board cell once and maintain only the count variable.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count battleships made of straight X runs on a board where ships never touch; each ship can be counted at its top-leftmost cell.
Idea: An empty outer array returns zero. The nested loops increment count for an X only if there is no X immediately above and no X immediately to its left.
Technique and why it applies: Top-left start detection counts each straight ship once without extra visited storage or altering board cells.
Invariant: Every previously scanned X belongs to a ship whose start has already been counted if it has no X above or left; continuation cells are skipped.
Edge cases: Empty boards return zero; a single X counts once; a vertical or horizontal ship contributes only at its first cell. board[0] is accessed only after the empty-row check, and rectangular input is assumed.
Complexity: Each cell is tested once, yielding O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops scan the board once and use only integer dimensions and the count accumulator.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum XOR of any two array values; the implementation greedily tests candidate bits from bit 31 down to bit 0.
Idea: For each bit, mask includes all bits considered so far and candidate sets that bit in ans. A set of x&mask prefixes is built; if some pair of prefixes XORs to candidate, ans adopts the bit.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy prefix testing determines each high-order answer bit if two values with the retained prefixes can realize it, fixing the most significant bits first.
Invariant: ans contains the largest feasible prefix chosen so far, and prefixes contains every input value masked to the bits examined so far.
Edge cases: A singleton array yields zero; duplicate values cannot create a positive XOR by themselves; the fixed 32-bit loop assumes the problem's nonnegative 32-bit integer range.
Complexity: There are 32 rounds with O(n) set construction and lookup, giving O(32n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The method rebuilds a prefix set from n values for each of 32 bit positions, requiring O(n) temporary storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the maximum XOR pair by deciding the answer from its most significant bit to its least significant bit.
Idea: Each iteration adds a bit to mask and proposes candidate=ans|(1<<bit). The set p contains every x&mask. The inner loop checks whether p contains candidate^x for any x; if so, ans keeps the candidate bit.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-mask greedy testing asks whether two masked values can XOR to the proposed prefix, allowing high-order bits to be fixed safely first.
Invariant: ans is the best feasible XOR prefix selected so far, and p represents all input prefixes under the current mask.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns zero; equal values XOR to zero; bit 31 uses Java's signed int representation but bitwise equality remains valid for the usual nonnegative constraints. The fixed 32 rounds match int width.
Complexity: Each of 32 rounds builds and checks an O(n) set, giving O(32n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The code scans nums to build p and scans p for complements during each of 32 bit trials.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reconstruct the sorted digit string from shuffled letters spelling digit names; each digit name has a letter that identifies it uniquely at a particular elimination stage.
Idea: Counter counts letters. Counts of z,w,u,x,g determine digits 0,2,4,6,8; counts of h,f,s then determine 3,5,7 after subtracting 8,4,6. Finally o determines 1 and i determines 9 after removing their overlapping digits. The output repeats each digit by its count in ascending order.
Technique and why it applies: Unique-letter elimination uses letters exclusive to certain digit names, then subtracts counts contributed by already-decoded names.
Invariant: Each d[i] is the number of occurrences of digit i implied by the letters processed so far, and later formulas remove overlap from already-counted digit names.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string; mixed digit names are resolved in dependency order; output is sorted because i increases from 0 to 9. Input is assumed to be a valid concatenation of English digit names.
Complexity: Counter construction and output generation are O(n) time; the alphabet and ten digit counters use O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The input is counted once and each decoded digit occurrence is appended once; Counter and d have fixed-size alphabet/digit state.

notes:
Task and constraints: Recover digits from a shuffled concatenation of English digit names, returning the digits in ascending order; the input uses lowercase letters.
Idea: c counts each letter in a 26-entry array. d[0], d[2], d[4], d[6], and d[8] use unique letters z,w,u,x,g. The method subtracts those counts to compute 3,5,7, then 1 and 9, and appends each digit j times in ascending order.
Technique and why it applies: Unique-letter elimination solves digits with exclusive letters first, then removes their contributions from shared letters to recover remaining digits.
Invariant: Each d[i] stores the inferred count of digit i after accounting for letter overlaps from previously resolved digits.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string; output is ordered because the final loop advances i from zero to nine; c[x-'a'] assumes lowercase English input. StringBuilder avoids repeated immutable concatenation.
Complexity: Counting and building the output take O(n) time; the 26-letter array and ten digit counts use O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The code scans s once and appends each output digit occurrence once, while the character and digit count arrays are fixed size.
